author: Anthropic
title: The Anthropic Economic Index
central_scenario_summary: An empirical measurement initiative, not a forecast: roughly one million Claude.ai conversations are mapped to O*NET occupational tasks to track how AI is actually used in the economy. Current usage is concentrated in software development and writing; about 36% of occupations use AI in at least a quarter of their tasks (only 4% in three-quarters or more); use tilts slightly toward augmentation (57%) over automation (43%); and usage peaks in mid-to-high-wage occupations while being low at both the bottom and very top of the wage distribution. Anthropic expects AI to have a major impact on work and plans longitudinal tracking, suggesting jobs may evolve rather than disappear if task-level diffusion patterns persist.

quotes.text: In the coming years, AI systems will have a major impact on the ways people work.
AI use is rapidly expanding, and models are becoming ever-more capable. The labor-market picture may look quite different within a relatively short time.

capability_pace.notes: The report deliberately avoids forecasting ('We don't... attempt to forecast the future'); scored 2 only for its framing of AI as a major economy-wide technology comparable to prior GPT waves.

expertise_erosion.notes: No position on entry barriers or expertise premia; wage-related finding is about usage rates, not returns to skill.

quotes.text: Today, usage is concentrated in software development and technical writing tasks. Over one-third of occupations (roughly 36%) see AI use in at least a quarter of their associated tasks
AI was diffused across the many tasks in the economy, having stronger impacts for some groups of tasks than others
quotes.location: Results, 'Depth of AI use within occupations'

productivity_breadth.notes: Describes observed current diffusion (concentrated but non-trivially widespread) rather than a forecast of eventual breadth.

quotes.text: AI use leans more toward augmentation (57%), where AI collaborates with and enhances human capabilities, compared to automation (43%), where AI directly performs tasks.
the future might be one where most current jobs evolve rather than disappear

substitution.notes: Mixed with a slight augmentation lean in current usage data; the report notes the automation share should be monitored over time.

demand_absorption.notes: Silent on demand-side absorption of productivity gains.

mobility_adjustment.notes: Silent on worker reallocation and retraining.

rent_concentration.notes: Silent on who captures the surplus.

timeline_years.notes: No stated timeline; only that the picture 'may look quite different within a relatively short time.'

inequality_prediction.score: The report makes no inequality prediction. Its distribution-relevant finding is that current AI use is highest in mid-to-high-wage occupations (e.g., programmers, data scientists) and low at both the lowest- and highest-paid roles, reflecting current capability limits and adoption barriers — implying uneven exposure across the wage distribution.

quotes.text: AI use is more prevalent for tasks associated with mid-to-high wage occupations like computer programmers and data scientists, but is lower for both the lowest- and highest-paid roles.

inequality_prediction.notes: Descriptive, not predictive; the initiative explicitly declines policy prescriptions and forecasts.
